title: A Guide to Truck-Mounted Crane Installation
excerpt: And so, you have a powerful truck-mounted crane that is ready to take your business to new heights—literally! But before you can start hoisting materials around like a construction maestro, there's an important part left, that is, installation.
content:
And so, you have a powerful truck-mounted crane that is ready to take your business to new heights—literally! But before you can start hoisting materials around like a construction maestro, there's an important part left, that is, installation. A methodical procedure of setting up a crane. It may seem convincingly simple, but there is no room for errors.

One wrong move and things can go south faster than a dropped load of bricks. We're talking financial woes, crew safety hazards, and even lawsuits – yikes! So, how do you navigate this process like a seasoned pro? Let's break it down.


Compatibility Check: Locating the Perfect Match for Your Truck

Your crane needs a properly matched truck chassis to work well. Consider these factors:

Crane Weight Rating: It tells how much weight your crane can safely pick up. Check that against the carrying capacity of your truck, so it does not overload: this means instability and no balance, both ends for the vehicle and crane.

Truck Frame Strength: Because trucks are not all created equally and differ in their strength, make sure that your truck frame will withstand the huge amount of force exerted by the crane when in operation.

A crane installation that throws the truck's center of gravity off-kilter is a disaster about to happen. It is important that the weight be well balanced in relation to the chassis and the weight over the crane.

Pro Tip: Have a discussion with a dealer that specializes in certified crane installations. Not only will they survey your truck, but they will also recommend the best crane fit so that your working relationship can be harmonious and safe.


Building a Good Base: The Benefits of a Subframe

For most serious cranes, however, it is usually the subframe that the unsung hero of the installation. The custom-fit steel structure is made to fit between the truck's chassis and the crane in order to spread the weight out and reinforce the frame of the truck.

Here's why a subframe may be your best bet:

Enhanced Stability: A supporting frame enhances the capability of the truck to manage the weight and leverage of the crane.

Reduced Strain: By spreading the load, the supporting frame reduces strain, on the trucks structure preventing harm.

Lasting Durability: A crafted supporting frame prolongs the lifespan of both your truck and crane.

Not all cranes necessitate a supporting frame. Lighter duty cranes may attach directly to the chassis. However, for cranes investing in a supporting frame is prudent for safety and long-term equipment wellbeing.


Securing the Crane: Installation and Fastening

Now is the moment when the crane is mounted on a truck. This involves attention to detail and expertise. This is an overview:

Accurate positioning: The crane is placed with absolute precision on the truck chassis to ensure that it is balanced and properly aligned.

Strong attachments: The crane has strong bolts and fasteners that strongly connect it either to its supporting frame or chassis as well.

Full checkup: Every joint, weld, and bolt go through a comprehensive scrutiny

Remember; Trained professionals who are experienced in handling machinery should be allowed to do this.


Linking the Hydraulics and Electrical Systems - Power Up

The secret behind how a crane moves lies within the system of which it is made. Here’s how it happens;

Hydraulic Connection: Hoses and pipes connect the crane's hydraulic system to the truck's power source, typically a Power Take Off (PTO) unit linked to the engine.

Electrical Integration:  Electrical wiring establishes communication between the crane's controls and the truck's electrical system, enabling operation.

Hydraulic Fluid: Not all fluids are created equal. Using the right hydraulic fluid is critical for smooth operation and protecting the crane's internal components. Imagine using the wrong oil in your car's engine – it could lead to friction and breakdowns. The chosen hydraulic fluid should be specifically designed for crane applications to withstand high pressures and ensure optimal performance.


Testing

Once the installation is complete, tough testing must be done. This is what to expect:

Functional Testing: Tests of all crane functions should be conducted adequately; from lift, lower, extend, and retract to swing.

Safety Checks: All safety functionalities including limit switches and overload protection systems should be tested completely.

Documentation: There will be a comprehensive account of how this was installed; the test results as well as certifications for future reference.


Wrap Up

Never can you ignore having tests! It’s the last step before your crane is ready to be put into action with confidence that ensures your crew’s safety and guarantees success in your project.

Those steps coupled with help from professionals in the field can transform your truck mounted cranes in to dependable machine in any sort of truck mounted crane related gigs.

title: Structure of Marine Cranes
excerpt: The captivating picture of a huge ship moving across the sea is an example of human ingenuity. But beneath the surface there is a network of complicated machinery that keeps these leviathans on the move – cranes always present.
content:
The captivating picture of a huge ship moving across the sea is an example of human ingenuity. But beneath the surface there is a network of complicated machinery that keeps these leviathans on the move – cranes always present. These industrial workhorses come in different forms and sizes but all share a common core structure designed for each part. Let us now consider the anatomy of these marine marvels.


The Base: Pedestal and Tower

At its base, a marine crane has its foundation which offers stability and contains critical constituents. Here comes the pedestal. Imagine a solid, cylindrical column securely fixed to the deck of any ocean-going vessel or barge.

This is referred to as the pedestal made from high-strength marine-grade steel that can stand against saltwater corrosion, wind, and waves in perpetuity. Inside this pedestal lies the slewing mechanism which can be thought of as being akin to “muscles” since they enable it to turn in full 360 degrees.” This mechanism makes use of powerful hydraulic motors or electric drives to ensure smooth sliding from one point to another.

In bigger cranes, there is a tall structure termed a tower mounted above a pedestal. The vertical post adds further height and range enabling the crane to lift heavier loads over longer distances. Normally a tower uses lattice work made up of steel beams offering more flexibility and balance between weight and strength.


The Lifting Arm: The Boom and its Maneuvering Magic

The crane’s boom remains the most conspicuous part of it. This lengthy, crosswise arm stretches either from the tower or directly from the pedestal (in smaller cranes) to make it possible for it to reach out and lift cargo. Booms of cranes have different types depending on their structure:

Fixed Boom: A design where there is an unchangeable length and lifting capacity. It can be used on certain ship cranes.

Telescopic Boom: A multi-purpose variant that has nested parts that are extendable hydraulically and then contracted intending to adapt its reach. These are perfect for port operations where cranes must adjust themselves according to the size of ships.

Knuckle Boom: common on workboats or barges, this design has a hinged joint at its base, enabling more exactitude in handling and moving around barriers.

Regardless of what type they may be, the booms are engineering marvels that are composed of high-strength steel material carefully designed to bear heavy loads yet remain steady. The boom can withstand all forces associated with bending and twisting during the lifting process because there are internal reinforcements as well as strategic weight distribution in its construction.


The Lifting Powerhouse: Winches and Hoisting Systems

It is the hoisting system that functions as the magical ingredient in lifting heavy objects. Comprising a robust winch, wire rope and a hook. Powered by either hydraulics or electric motors, the winch is the mainstay that coils up the wire rope thus moving up and down. Wire rope made of high-quality steel filaments acts as “muscle” for transmitting pulling force from winch to load. Lastly, hook, a strong steel fitting that connects cargo being lifted.

In many cases, modern cranes have incorporated advanced features into their hoisting system. By limiting the loads, it ensures that no crane will go out of its safe working range of operation.

When there’s more than one weight being lifted at once, anti-two-block collision technology helps prevent accidental damage due to hitting something together with them while they are rising upwards. Additionally, some cranes boast variable speed control for precise maneuvering of the load.


Sway Control and Counterweights: Keeping it Steady

Cranes that operate on vessels such as ships and barges face a unique challenge – how to stay steady on such rocking platforms? And this is where sway control comes in handy. These systems employ hydraulic actuators and sensors to detect and counteract any swinging motion of both the boom arm and payload. Through applying opposite forces, sway control makes sure that even when faced with tough sea conditions lifting operations will be smooth and safe for all staff involved throughout this entire course.

Another critical design consideration for stability is the counterbalance. This massive inertial mass usually of concrete or steel blocks, is placed at the back of a crane. The weight of the boom and lifted goods are leveled by the counterbalance so that no tipping over will occur to the crane. The appropriate location as well as the weight of this counterbalance is significant since it maintains a safe center of gravity within the crane.


Conclusion

Marine cranes are not simply pieces of metal; they form an orchestra of might, accuracy and engineering excellence. All their constituents starting from bulky pedestals up to sophisticated hoisting systems interact harmoniously with one another towards achieving only one goal - efficient and safe lifting works in marine conditions characterized by high demand for services.

Understanding their structure allows for a deeper appreciation of these workhorses of the sea, the silent heroes keeping global trade and maritime operations flowing smoothly.

title: Best Crane Safety Tips to Prevent Accidents
excerpt: Tall cranes play a role in the construction sites lifting materials and reshaping city skylines effortlessly. However, this great power comes with risks.
content:
Tall cranes play a role in the construction sites lifting materials and reshaping city skylines effortlessly. However, this great power comes with risks. A single mistake can lead to life ending consequences. Fear not! By focusing on safety and following these crane safety guidelines you can establish a work environment and ensure your projects progress smoothly without accidents.



The Importance of Preparation: Planning is Key

Even the experienced crane operator can only succeed with a thought-out plan. Here's how to prepare for an operation;

Pre Lift-Briefing: Hold a team meeting, before each lift. Discuss the load weight lifting path, potential dangers, and the roles of designated signalers. Clear communication is essential.

Lift Plan Creation: Develop a lift plan that covers all aspects of the operation including weight restrictions, sling choices, and assigned personnel responsibilities.

Site Examination: Before every lift carefully inspect the work area. Identify any obstructions, power lines, or unstable ground conditions that could be hazardous.

Expert Tip: Don't hesitate to delay the lift if unexpected situations arise. Safety should always come first over sticking to the schedule.



Understanding Boundaries: Respecting Capacity and Capability

Cranes are engineering wonders but they have their limits.

To stay safe while operating a crane keep these tips in mind;

●       Know the crane's lifting capacity. Never go over it to avoid any accidents.

●       Make sure to weigh the load or get an expert opinion, on its weight before lifting it.

●       Understand that as the load moves away from the crane boom its lifting capacity decreases. Stick, to the working radius to prevent any mishaps.

Remember: It's better to use a larger crane with ample capacity than to push the limits of a smaller one.



The Stabilizing Force: Setting Up for Success

To make sure that a crane is safe when operating, its stability is very essential. Here’s how to do it.

Outrigger Deployment: Always completely extend and position the crane’s outriggers rightly on solid flat ground. On soft surfaces, use outrigger pads to enhance stability.

Ground Conditions: A crane should never be used on uneven, unstable, or soft grounds. Look for ground that can support the weight of the load and the crane itself.

Leveling the Crane: Before lifting operations begin, use spirit levels to make sure that the crane is perfectly level.

Pro Tip: Make regular inspections on outriggers for damages and ensure that they move freely before you use them every time.



Clear Signals for Safe Operations – Communication is King

Miscommunication is a recipe for disaster during a crane operation. Here’s how to make sure everyone gets it:

Designated Signaler: Only one crew member who can be easily seen by everybody must give signals to the crane operator.

Standardized Signals: To avoid any misinterpretation, use worldwide accepted hand signs or an approved radio communication system.

Operator Awareness: All signals must first be acknowledged and understood by the crane operator before proceeding with any lifting maneuver.

Pro Tip: Train your crew regularly in proper hand signaling as well as communication protocols.



The All-Seeing Eye: Maintaining Visibility Throughout the Lift

Safety is important in the entire lifting exercise and a good view of it should be able to see the whole process. Here’s how to get optimal visibility:

Identification And Removal of Blind Spots: Locate and eliminate any blind spots along the lifting path, move people around, or use mirrors to improve vision.

Overhead Hazards: Incline cranes, power lines, other cranes, and anything that might collide with the load.

Safe Workers: Keep team members far from crane areas and load paths not directly affected by uplifts.

Pro Tip: Use a spotter where visibility is limited during loading operations.



The Final Line of Defense: Safety Gear

Even with meticulous planning and procedures, accidents will nevertheless occur. This is how potential injuries may be minimized:

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Proper PPE must be worn by each member of the crew including hard hats, safety glasses, and work boots.

Falling Object Protection: Always wear a hard hat when working under lifted loads and stay away from rigging to avoid injury from falling materials.

Lifting Slings and Gear: Inspect slings for damage regularly and ensure they are rated above the weight capacity of the load being lifted.

Keep in mind that safety gear does not take the place of proper procedures but it can be extremely helpful when unexpected things happen.



Wrap Up

You can create a work environment where everybody returns home safe and sound at the end of each day by putting in place these essential crane safety tips. Remember, safety is everyone’s responsibility.

You ensure smooth running and efficient operations of your crane by using effective communication channels, continuous training programs and best practices commitment therefore ensuring timely completion of your projects while securing the lives of your team members.

title: Differences between Truck Mounted Cranes And Mobile Cranes
excerpt: Differences between Truck Mounted Cranes And Mobile Cranes, BOB-LIFT
content:
A crane is an essential equipment in construction. Construction projects ranging from high rise apartments, bridges and factories rely heavily on different types of cranes as they can perform lifting tasks that humans cannot manage. That said, it is important to carefully evaluate a crane’s operational abilities mainly because of the extensive crane variety available today.

Truck mounted cranes and mobile cranes are favored options with a parallel general function. However, they provide unique features, operation and advantages. Let’s delve into the key differences of these two main types of cranes.



Truck Mounted Crane

A truck mounted crane is a heavy-duty construction equipment used for projects that involve hoisting, lowering and adjusting. The mounted crane design ensures strong heavy duty lifting and easy mobility even in long distance transportation.

Advantages


Multi-purpose

Truck mounted cranes allow for multiple functions like loading, unloading and transportation. This advantage reduces the additional cost one would incur while using two crane types. Our high-quality truck mounted cranes match the reliability of two machines.


Better Site Accessibility

Truck mounted crane designs consist of a chassis body that offers enhanced efficiency when it comes to site accessibility. You can easily transport them on main and public roads to access sites unreachable with other cranes.


Speedy

There are speed limitations that apply to certain cranes on main roads. These speed limitations do not apply to truck mounted cranes, which means enhanced work efficiency through timely arrival at the project site.

* Please observe speed limitations according to your local laws.


Shorter Set-up Time

A great advantage of a truck mounted crane is that it does not require a lot of time to erect before operation. The preparation time is shorter as it is parked at the working position then counterbalanced before beginning the task.



Truck Mounted Crane Specialty & Functions

● Easy transportation to and from construction sites

● High capacity ideal for heavy lifting

● Practical and easy to set up

● Used for hoisting heavy duty loads







Mobile Cranes

Mobile cranes refer to a self-propelled lifting equipment. The boom and hoist of the crane are fixed on wheels and the operator uses the vehicle's driving controls to move the crane to position. A mobile crane also has food pads that ensure enhanced stability during a task.

This type of cranes come in a smaller size compared to fixed cranes, but gigantic models are available.





Advantages

Mobility

Unlike tower cranes that are set up in a fixed position, you can easily move around a mobile crane when set up on a vehicle. For this reason, improved maneuverability is a key advantage that makes mobile cranes a popular option - they are speedy and efficient in a construction project.

Smaller Footprint

Mobile cranes can be easily transported on both local and main roads. They are smaller in size hence can be transported in limited space. Their compact size also ensures easy passage under low bridges and does not cause unnecessary traffic.

Fast Setup

A mobile crane is set up on wheels, reducing the set-up requirements on a construction site. This means you can start your projects in a timely and efficient manner. You can also save on hiring costs as they are on your construction site for a shorter period.

Higher Level of Strength

Despite the compact size of a mobile crane, they provide the high strength required to complete hoisting tasks. Their sturdiness can be attributed to features like heavy duty axles and incredible strength which enable safe handling of loads.


Mobile Cranes Specialty & Function

● Enhanced mobility and compatibility with varying carrier types

● Higher capacity than tower cranes and convenient for heavy loads

● Used to hoist heavy duty materials that cannot be lifted using low-capacity cranes

● Easy to operate and require less set-up time


Mounted Cranes vs. Mobile Cranes: Which Is Better for Your Business?

The unique needs of your construction project should guide your choice between a truck-mounted crane or a mobile crane. A truck-mounted crane will provide excellent mobility, fast set up and easy transportation to various sites

A mobile crane is an ideal choice if your project requires a crane with top notch lifting capacity and elevated reach capabilities.

Whichever your preference, safety is key. Our equipment meets safety and regulatory standards. Nevertheless, the operator should be well trained and certified in handling cranes.


Take Away

At BOB-LIFT, we boast a large fleet of optimum quality and other crane types, while offering exceptional after sales. We are committed to providing our customers with machinery that suits different project needs. For more enquiries on truck mounted cranes vs mobile cranes or information on features and specs contact BOB-LIFT today.

title: Lifting Capacity of Knuckle Boom Cranes
excerpt: Lifting Capacity of Knuckle Boom Cranes, BOB-LIFT
content:
In the world of lifting operations, knuckle boom cranes operate like multi equipped Swiss Army knives by being powerful and versatile yet compact in size. The articulated arm of modern knuckle boom cranes allows folded extension thus enabling them to handle loads more precisely inside limited locations. We need to assess the max lifting capability of knuckle boom cranes when dealing with heavy loads.


The exact weight restriction for knuckle boom cranes exists beyond one simple metric. Multiple variables determine a knuckle boom crane's lifting ability because they encompass how the boom extends and which hydraulic system it uses together with stability mechanics and load placement.


The process of finding the appropriate crane requires knowledge about boom length and hydraulic power and stability and load positioning parameters among other elements for everyone operating in construction or logistics or industrial transport sectors.


Knuckle Boom Lifting Capacity Evaluation

Each crane represents its lifting capabilities through a unique load chart that specifies multiple working conditions for lifting capacity. Knuckle boom cranes maintain the same conditions when it comes to understanding their lifting capacity. Ton-meters represent the technical measurement of capacity since it combines both load weight with reach length of the boom structure.

For example:

With a 20 ™ crane the operator can lift 20 tons whenever the rig stands at 1 meter from the ground.

The lifting capacity goes down when the boom length reaches 5 meters because of how leverage affects the weight distribution.

The actual lifting power of a crane depends on the reach distance it must extend, and the positioning method used for the material.



Factors Affecting Lifting Capacity

Various factors decide the maximum safe weight capacity of knuckle boom cranes.

Boom Length and Angle

The lifting capacity of knuckle boom crane equipment rises when the boom stands straight up because vertical orientation needs minimal counterbalancing forces. Extending a boom completely makes the load heavier because the leverage effect increases the stress placed on hydraulic mechanisms.

Hydraulic Power and Stability

The power output of hydraulic cylinders increases with their mechanical strength which results in increased lifting capabilities.

Safe operations during heavy load handling occur when a crane maintains proper stability through outrigger deployment and mount base implementation.

Load Distribution

The lifting of symmetrically distributed weight proves much simpler than attempts to lift irregular shapes. A proper placement of loads will determine stability since weights must be distributed evenly when loads sit off-center.


Environmental Conditions

Wind speed together with soil or ground conditions can affect the stability of the crane system during operations. The lifting limits become unsafe when operating on terrain which is not level or contains unsteady surfaces.


Typical Lifting Capacities by Crane Size

Choosing the suitable knuckle boom crane depends on precisely how much power is needed to execute the planned task.

The requirements for basic maintenance work and light duty transport can be served with cranes that measure 5–10 tm and handle lift to 3 tons.

Medium cranes ranging from 10–30 tm lift 3 to 10 tons which proves ideal for construction projects and agricultural scenes and utility company operations. Large cranes (30–100 tm) effortlessly lift 10 to 30+ tons since they excel at industrial transport and marine operations.

The extra heavy crane category (100+ tm) rules the operational fields of mining along with port activities and oil and gas industries through its ability to handle 30+ tons effortlessly.

The mere size of a crane does not determine its lifting capacity. The maximum lifting capacity of a 30-tm knuckle boom crane reaches 12 tons when the boom measures 2.5 meters long but extends the reach to 5 meters to restrict the lift to 6 tons.

This situation demonstrates one of the common physical laws at work. Distance extends from the crane significantly affects the maximum weight you should lift during operation. The selection process goes beyond weight limits since the operating distance becomes important in a crane choice.



Selecting an Appropriate Knuckle Boom Crane

1. Determine the heaviest weight your lifting operations require. You should select a crane which has a rating capacity greater than 20% above your maximum lifting weight.

2. The reach range of your boom determines the crane selection because you can verify the required reach with a load chart analysis for adequate performance.

3. The mounting surface of the crane needs evaluation. A solid mounting base including trucks, stationary units and naval ships determines the crane's operational safety levels.

4. You must establish what type of attachments will be used for the job. Changes between grapples and winches and rotators directly determine the efficiency of load management.


Safety Considerations for Maximum Lifting Efficiency

A crane maintains no value when safety standards are disregarded during operation. Best practices in operation protect efficiency and maintain safety performance.

● Always check load charts. Make sure to check load capacity before operating because cranes must not be assumed able to lift any load.

● Use outriggers properly. Outriggers must be set in proper locations where the ground is stable.

● Monitor hydraulic pressure. The excessive force of overloading creates deterioration within hydraulic components which shortens their operating duration.

● Train operators thoroughly. The right level of operator skill allows personnel to deliver better operational results with reduced dangers.



Final Thoughts

The modern market offers knuckle boom cranes as the most adaptable solutions for efficient lifting operations. The lifting ability of these machines depends on different variables which include hydraulic power together with the length of the boom as well as the position of the load.

Given knowledge of these fundamental factors anyone can achieve peak operational safety and productivity when using boom cranes for lifting loads of all sizes.

title: Five Steps To Select A "fitting" Tailboard for Your Truck

content:
Installing the tail plate is not that complicated. Just follow these five steps and you can easily lock in the one that suits you best. 


Step 1: Determine the load capacity

Choose 1.2 times the maximum weight of a single piece of cargo as the standard.

For common goods, 1 ton is usually used, so select the 1.5-ton specification; for common forklift pallet loads, it is recommended to start with 2 tons.

Choosing too small is risky, while choosing too large is a waste. 


Step 2: Measure the height of the vehicle compartment

Measure three values: the height of the vehicle compartment from the ground, the width of the compartment, and the rear space.

If the distance from the ground exceeds 1.3 meters, a long type should be chosen. If it is lower than 0.7 meters, a folding type is recommended to avoid damaging the tailboard when it is unfolded.

Special attention should be paid to van-type vehicles: Make sure the tailboard does not block the tail lights and license plate when it is folded. 



Step 3: Confirm the vehicle type

Truck with box body: Limited space, folding type is preferred

Flatbed truck: Loose installation is acceptable, vertical or cantilever type is fine

Light truck/mini truck: Thin frame, small battery, lightweight aluminum tailboard is the priority

Let us know your vehicle type, frame width and battery voltage in advance. This will help us confirm if it can be installed. 


Step 4: Choose the material - Steel or Aluminum?

Steel tailboards: They are heavier but have a lower price and are durable, suitable for heavy goods, construction materials, and harsh working conditions.

Aluminum tailboards: They are lighter and do not rust, suitable for light trucks, seafood cold chain, and users who are sensitive to weight.

In a nutshell: Choose steel for heavy tasks, aluminum for light tasks, and aluminum for seafood transportation. 



Step 5: Confirm power supply and control

Voltage: Light-duty trucks and vans typically use 12V, while medium and heavy-duty trucks use 24V. They must be compatible.

Control: Wired hand controllers are the most reliable, while wireless remote controls are the most convenient. Choose based on personal preference.

Regardless of the choice, an emergency stop button must be included. 


Select the tail plate and follow these five steps: load capacity → height → vehicle model → material → power supply. Follow these steps carefully and you won't go wrong.

title: What Are The Differences between Knuckle Boom And Telescopic Boom Truck Cranes?
excerpt: What Are The Differences between Knuckle Boom And Telescopic Boom Truck Cranes?, BOB-LIFT
content:
The knuckle boom and the telescopic boom, these two types of vehicle-mounted cranes do not have an absolute "better" one. Instead, each has its own characteristics and advantages, and is suitable for different working conditions and operation requirements.

I. What is a knuckle-boom truck crane?

A knuckle boom truck crane, as the name suggests, has a boom that can be folded and extended in multiple sections like "joints". Its structure is more flexible and its movements are more delicate. It usually uses a hydraulic system for precise control and can perform multi-angle lifting operations.

The main advantages of the knuckle boom:

1. Flexible operation, suitable for complex working conditions

The greatest feature of the knuckle boom is its high flexibility. It can perform lifting operations in narrow spaces and environments with many obstacles, such as inside factories, urban streets, warehouse loading and unloading, and garden construction. In complex environments, the folding arm is more likely to be precisely positioned.

2. High operational accuracy, suitable for precise lifting

The knuckle boom operates more smoothly during lifting, making it suitable for tasks with high positioning accuracy requirements, such as transporting equipment, installing glass, and transporting precision materials. For construction tasks that require "stability, accuracy, and skillfulness", the folding arm often performs better.

3. Compact storage, higher space utilization of the entire vehicle

When the knuckle boom is in the retracted position, the overall structure is relatively compact, occupying the cabin space in a more reasonable manner. This not only facilitates transportation but is also more suitable for customers with specific requirements for the overall layout of the vehicle.

II. What is a telescopic boom truck crane?

A telescopic boom truck crane completes its work by extending the boom section by section outward. Its structure is relatively straightforward and its usage method is more traditional and widespread. It is very mature in applications such as basic engineering, construction transportation, and equipment handling.

The main advantages of the telescopic boom:

1. Simple structure, easier to use and maintain

The mechanical structure of the telescopic boom is relatively more straightforward, making it easier for users to operate and facilitating maintenance. For many customers who need to use the equipment frequently over a long period of time, the telescopic boom has strong practical value.

2. Fast lifting speed, high operational efficiency

In routine lifting tasks, the telescopic boom operation process is simple, and the actions of extending, lifting, and retraction are highly efficient. It is particularly suitable for high-frequency operation scenarios such as site loading and unloading, construction materials transportation, and general cargo lifting.

3. Large working radius, suitable for construction in open areas

The telescopic boom has a very obvious advantage in open spaces. It can quickly extend the boom to the target area and is suitable for construction sites, road construction, power engineering, logistics transportation and other environments that require a large working range.

III. Knuckle boom and telescopic boom, which customers are they suitable for?

If your working environment is complex, the construction location is restricted, and you have high requirements for lifting accuracy and flexibility, then a knuckle boom truck crane would be a more ideal choice. It is more suitable for precise operations and can better demonstrate the high performance and modern advantages of the equipment.

If your main requirements are for daily transportation and loading/unloading, construction engineering, and basic lifting operations, and you are seeking practicality, efficiency and economy, then a telescopic boom truck-mounted crane would be more suitable. It has a wide range of applications and strong adaptability, and is a mature model that many customers have long relied on.

Whether you need flexible and precise folding arms, or efficient and practical telescopic arms, BOB-LIFT is committed to being your reliable partner, helping make each lifting operation safer, more efficient and more convenient.

title: Marine Crane Buying Guide: Knuckle Boom vs Telescopic Boom and How to Size One
excerpt: How to choose a marine crane for your vessel: knuckle boom vs telescopic boom, how to read a load chart and how to size one to your deck.
content:
A marine crane is a slewing crane mounted on a vessel's deck to lift cargo, stores, equipment and small boats on and off the ship. Choosing one starts with three questions: how heavy is your heaviest lift, how far from the crane column does it hang, and how much deck space can the crane take up when it is not working.

This guide explains the two main boom types, how to read a load chart, how to size a crane to your vessel and what the rules say about certification. The figures quoted come from the load charts and specifications in BOB-LIFT's marine crane product manual, which covers 14 knuckle boom models from 0.8 to 25 t and 10 telescopic boom models from 2 to 20 t.

Key Takeaways

  • Knuckle boom marine cranes fold into a small footprint and place loads precisely in tight spaces. Telescopic boom cranes reach farther in a straight line. In BOB-LIFT's range, the telescopic model reaches farther than the knuckle model at every capacity offered in both types, and from 4 t upward it also has the higher lifting moment.
  • The headline tonnage is only available close to the column: about 2.0 to 2.25 m for most BOB-LIFT knuckle models and 2.5 m for most telescopic models. At full reach the same cranes lift between 200 kg and 2 t.
  • Size a crane by the load at your working radius, read from the load chart. Dividing the lifting moment by the radius gives a first estimate, but it overstates the load at long reach.
  • Check that the vessel can carry the crane's self-weight, base loads and power demand, not just the load.
  • Since 1 January 2026, SOLAS regulation II-1/3-13 sets rules for lifting appliances on ships it covers, so confirm what your vessel needs before ordering.

What is a marine crane?

A marine crane, also called a ship crane or deck crane, is a crane, usually hydraulic or electro-hydraulic, fixed to a pedestal on the deck of a vessel. It slews around its column and lifts with a boom and hook, so the crew can move loads between the deck, the quay and the water without shore equipment.

Deck-mounted marine cranes are different from the large gantry and ship-to-shore cranes used at ports, and from heavy offshore cranes built for platforms and construction vessels. For those distinctions, see our articles on the types of cranes used on a ship, the cranes used at docks and the differences between marine cranes and offshore cranes. This guide focuses on vessel-mounted cranes in the 0.8 to 25 t class.

Typical jobs for a crane of this size include:

  • Loading stores, spare parts, nets and gear from the quay.
  • Lifting cargo, containers of catch or equipment in and out of holds.
  • Launching and recovering tenders, workboats or small equipment. Launching lifeboats and rescue boats falls under separate life-saving appliance rules.
  • Handling tools and components during maintenance and repair.

Knuckle boom or telescopic boom: which suits your deck?

Both boom types are hydraulic, slew on a pedestal and lift with a hook. The difference is how the boom gets its reach, and that shapes how much deck the crane uses and where it can place a load.

Knuckle boom marine cranes

A knuckle boom marine crane has an inner boom and an outer boom joined by a hinge, like a finger. Hydraulic cylinders fold and unfold the two sections, and the outer boom usually carries telescopic extensions for extra reach.

The main advantages are:

  • Compact stowage. The boom folds back against the column, so the crane occupies little deck and is easy to secure for sea.
  • Precise placement. The folding joint lets the operator reach over a gunwale, into a hold or under an obstruction and set the load down gently. BOB-LIFT's manual describes a double four-bar linkage in the boom that lets it work at a reverse angle, which widens the working range.
  • Flexible working envelope. The hook can move up, out and down independently, which helps on crowded decks.

The trade-off is more moving parts. Every joint adds pins, bushings, cylinders and hoses to inspect and grease, and all of them sit in salt air.

Telescopic boom marine cranes

A telescopic boom marine crane has a straight main boom with sections that slide out of each other. A luffing cylinder raises and lowers the boom, and the extension cylinders set the reach.

The main advantages are:

  • Longer straight-line reach. The boom extends directly toward the load, which suits lifts over the side or onto a quay. In BOB-LIFT's range, the telescopic models reach 8.0 to 22.3 m, against 4.2 to 18 m for the knuckle models.
  • More lifting moment per tonne of rating. From 4 t upward, the telescopic model at each capacity has a higher lifting moment than the knuckle model, for example 25 against 21 t·m at 10 t.
  • Simpler boom geometry. There is one boom and one pivot, so there are fewer joints to maintain.

The trade-off is stowage. A telescopic boom cannot fold, so it needs a clear run of deck or a boom rest when lowered. The sliding sections and their wear pads also need regular attention in a marine environment.

Knuckle boom Telescopic boom
How it reaches Folds and unfolds at one or more joints Slides boom sections out in a straight line
Stowed footprint Small, folded against the column Longer, boom retracted and lowered
Best at Tight decks, placing loads into holds or under obstructions Clear decks, lifts over the side, longer straight reach
Maintenance focus Pins, bushings, hoses at each joint Sliding sections, wear pads, extension seals
BOB-LIFT range 14 models, 0.8 to 25 t, reach 4.2 to 18 m 10 models, 2 to 20 t, reach 8.0 to 22.3 m

How much can a marine crane lift? Reading the load chart

A marine crane's headline rating, such as "10 t", is the most it can lift, and only close to the column. What decides the load at longer reach is the lifting moment, the load multiplied by its horizontal distance from the slewing center, quoted in tonne-metres (t·m). The load chart turns that into a rated load at each working radius.

For a first estimate, divide the lifting moment by the radius you need:

estimated load (t) ≈ lifting moment (t·m) ÷ radius (m), never more than the rated capacity.

The load chart then gives the real figure. Take the 10 t knuckle boom marine crane, model SQ10ZA6TJ, rated at 21 t·m. Its chart gives 10 t at 2.0 m, 4.65 t at 4.5 m and 3.08 t at 6.49 m, close to the estimate of 3.2 t. At its full reach of 14.68 m it gives 1.15 t, well below the 1.4 t the estimate suggests, because the boom's own weight counts for more as it extends.

Telescopic cranes add one more variable. Their load charts are tables by boom length and boom angle, not a single curve. For the 10 t telescopic model, SQ10SA4T, the chart gives 5.7 t at a 4.3 m radius with the 5.6 m boom at 30°, but only 4.3 t at a 4.4 m radius with the 9.02 m boom raised to 60°. The radius is almost the same, but the longer boom weighs more, so it lifts less. Read the row for the boom length you will actually use.

For a lift plan, always use the manufacturer's load chart for the exact model and boom configuration. Our article on the lifting moment of a crane explains load charts and moment limiters in more detail.

What the load charts of BOB-LIFT's 24 models show

We read the load chart of every model in BOB-LIFT's marine crane product manual. Three patterns stand out:

  • Full rated load stops close to the column. Most knuckle models lift their full rating out to 2.0 to 2.25 m (the 0.8 t and 1.6 t models to about 1.3 to 1.4 m). Most telescopic models reach 2.5 m at full rating, and the 2 t and 3.2 t models 2.0 and 2.2 m.
  • Telescopic models reach farther. At every capacity offered in both types, the telescopic model has the longer maximum working radius, from 8.0 against 7.7 m at 4 t to 22.3 against 15.9 m at 16 t.
  • Loads at full reach are small. At the last point on each chart, the cranes lift between 200 kg (the 3.2 t telescopic model at 10.5 m) and 2 t (the 25 t knuckle model at 18 m).

The practical lesson is simple. If you need "3 t at 6 m", you need a crane with at least 18 t·m and a load chart that confirms 3 t at 6 m. In BOB-LIFT's range, the 10 t knuckle model gives 3.08 t at 6.49 m and the 8 t telescopic model, SQ8SA5T, gives 3.1 t at 6.0 m with its 8.8 m boom at 40°. The 8 t knuckle model, at 16.7 t·m, falls short, and its chart gives 2.47 t at 6.49 m. A 3.2 t crane, at 6.8 t·m, is nowhere near. Our guide to ways to calculate crane capacity covers the arithmetic step by step.

How to size a marine crane to your vessel

Size the crane from the job, then check that the vessel can carry the crane.

  1. Heaviest single lift. Weigh the heaviest item you will lift and add the hook block, slings and any lifting beam. This sets the capacity class.
  2. Radius of that lift. Measure the horizontal distance from where the crane column will stand to where that load must be picked up and set down, including over the side to the quay. Then check the load chart at that radius.
  3. Deck space and stowage. Check where the crane can be mounted and where the boom will rest at sea. A tight deck or a need to reach into a hold points to a knuckle boom. A clear run of deck and lifts over the side point to a telescopic boom.
  4. What the vessel can carry. BOB-LIFT marine cranes weigh from 220 kg for the 0.8 t knuckle model to 6,950 kg for the 20 t telescopic model. That weight sits high on the deck, and the crane's base and the deck beneath it must take the lifting loads. Ask a naval architect or the vessel's designer to confirm the mounting position and the effect on stability.
  5. Power supply. Across the range, BOB-LIFT lists a recommended power of 3.5 to 55 kW, hydraulic flow of 8 to 80 L/min (80 + 63 L/min on the 20 t telescopic model) and system pressure of 16 to 35 MPa. BOB-LIFT's manual shows both electric and diesel hydraulic power units. Confirm whether your vessel's own hydraulic system can supply the crane instead.
  6. Slewing range. All BOB-LIFT marine cranes from 2 t upward slew 360° continuously. The 0.8 t and 1.6 t knuckle models slew 330°. Check that the crane can reach every position you need from its mounting point.
  7. Options and controls. Decide early whether you need a winch, a grapple or a work basket, and whether the operator will work from an overhead seat or a wireless remote. BOB-LIFT also adapts the mounting arrangement to the vessel on request.

Matching capacity class to the job

The table below is a general guide to where each capacity band fits. The right model always depends on the load at your radius, not the headline rating.

Capacity class BOB-LIFT models Typical fit
0.8 to 3.2 t Knuckle 0.8, 1.6, 2, 3.2 t; telescopic 2, 3.2 t Small workboats, yachts and fishing boats handling stores, gear and light equipment
4 to 8 t Knuckle 4, 4.6, 5, 6.3, 8 t; telescopic 4, 5, 6.3, 8 t Fishing vessels and workboats lifting catch, nets, tenders and heavier equipment
10 to 16 t Knuckle 10, 12, 16 t; telescopic 10, 12, 16 t Barges and larger work vessels handling cargo and equipment
20 to 25 t Knuckle 20, 25 t; telescopic 20 t Barges and larger vessels with the deck strength and space for a heavy crane

Built for the sea: corrosion and sea conditions

Salt spray attacks paint, steel, hydraulic fittings and electrical connections, so a marine crane needs better protection than a crane that works on land.

BOB-LIFT's manual states that its marine cranes use several anti-rust processes designed for the marine environment. The product pages for several telescopic models, including the 2 t, 16 t and 20 t, specify an epoxy zinc-rich primer and a polyurethane acrylic topcoat to resist seawater corrosion, and sealed electrical components to keep moisture out. When you compare suppliers, ask for the coating system and film thickness, the hose and fitting specification, and how electrical parts are sealed.

Sea conditions also matter. The rating of a shipboard crane assumes the vessel is close to level. Lifting while the vessel heels, trims or moves in a swell swings the load and adds dynamic force to the crane and the vessel. Ask any supplier what heel and trim its ratings allow, and plan lifts for sheltered water whenever you can.

For a closer look at pedestals, booms, winches and counterweights, read the structure of marine cranes.

Rules and certification to check before you buy

Whether your marine crane needs certification depends on the vessel, its flag and its class, so check this before you order.

SOLAS regulation II-1/3-13. The International Maritime Organization added this regulation on lifting appliances and anchor handling winches, and it entered into force on 1 January 2026. It covers design, construction, operation, inspection, testing and maintenance. Its design, construction and installation requirements apply to ships built on or after 1 January 2026, while its operation, inspection, testing and maintenance requirements apply to all ships it covers (IMCA Information Note 1657, January 2024). Lloyd's Register notes that new lifting appliances must be certified before entering service, including plan appraisal, material verification, inspection and a load test once installed (Lloyd's Register class news 12/2025). For appliances with a safe working load below 1,000 kg, the flag state decides how far the design, construction and installation provisions apply (IMCA).

Which ships SOLAS covers. Unless a regulation says otherwise, SOLAS applies to ships on international voyages, and its general exceptions include cargo ships under 500 gross tonnage, fishing vessels, pleasure yachts not engaged in trade and ships not propelled by mechanical means (SOLAS consolidated edition, Chapter I, regulations 1 and 3). National rules, the vessel's classification society or a charterer can still require a certified crane on a vessel outside SOLAS.

Before you order. If your vessel is classed or falls under SOLAS, including when you add a crane to an existing ship, confirm the requirements with your flag administration and classification society.

Installation, operation and maintenance

A marine crane is only as safe as its mounting and its daily care. The deck must be reinforced for the crane's base loads, the pedestal bolted or welded to an approved design, and the hydraulic and electrical connections protected from spray.

In service, keep these habits:

  • Check the load chart for every lift. Know the load weight and the radius before you lift. BOB-LIFT marine cranes carry a dedicated moment limiter, but it is a safeguard, not a substitute for planning the lift.
  • Keep people clear. Never stand under the boom or a suspended load.
  • Stow and secure the boom at sea. An unsecured boom can swing as the vessel rolls.
  • Inspect before use. Look at hoses, cylinders, pins, the hook latch and the slewing ring bolts, and grease the joints as the manual specifies.
  • Rinse and touch up. Wash salt off after use and repair paint damage before rust spreads.

Our guide to safely putting marine cranes on ships covers installation planning in more detail.

Frequently asked questions

Is a knuckle boom or telescopic boom marine crane better for a small deck?

A knuckle boom is usually the better fit for a small or crowded deck. It folds against its column when stowed and can place loads into holds or under obstructions. A telescopic boom needs a clear run of deck to lower and rest its boom, but it reaches farther and, in BOB-LIFT's range from 4 t upward, has a higher lifting moment at the same rated capacity.

What does "10 t, 21 t·m" mean on a marine crane?

The first figure is the rated capacity, the most the crane can lift, available only close to the column. The second is the lifting moment, the load multiplied by its radius. On BOB-LIFT's 10 t knuckle model, SQ10ZA6TJ, the load chart gives 10 t at 2.0 m, 3.08 t at 6.49 m and 1.15 t at 14.68 m. Always read the load chart for the radius you need.

How far can a marine crane reach?

It depends on the model and boom type. In BOB-LIFT's range, the knuckle boom models reach 4.2 to 18 m and the telescopic boom models 8.0 to 22.3 m. At full reach they lift only a small part of their rating, between 200 kg and 2 t, so check the load at the reach you need.

Do marine cranes need classification society certification?

It depends on the vessel. SOLAS regulation II-1/3-13, in force since 1 January 2026, sets certification, testing and maintenance rules for lifting appliances on ships covered by SOLAS. Many smaller cargo ships, fishing vessels and pleasure yachts fall outside SOLAS, but national or class rules can still apply. Confirm your vessel's requirements first.

How is a marine crane powered?

BOB-LIFT marine cranes are hydraulic. Each model lists a recommended power, from 3.5 kW for the 0.8 t knuckle model to 55 kW for the 25 t knuckle and the 16 t and 20 t telescopic models, plus the hydraulic flow and pressure it needs. BOB-LIFT offers electric and diesel hydraulic power units, or you can check whether the vessel's own hydraulic system has the capacity.

What should I send to get a marine crane quote?

Send the heaviest load, the radius you need it at, the vessel type and size, the planned mounting position and deck space, and the power available on board. With those details, BOB-LIFT can recommend a model and send its load chart. You can send an inquiry or contact the team.

Choosing the right marine crane

The right marine crane is the one that lifts your heaviest load at your working radius, fits your deck when stowed and suits what your vessel can carry.

  • Choose a knuckle boom for tight decks and precise placement, or a telescopic boom for clear decks and longer straight reach.
  • Size by the load chart at your radius, not by the headline tonnage.
  • Confirm deck strength, stability, power supply and certification requirements before you order.

title: Forklift Jib Crane Guide: How a Fly Jib Turns Your Forklift Into a Crane
excerpt: What a forklift jib crane is, how hydraulic fly jibs differ from simple fork jibs, how capacity falls with reach, and how to match one to your forklift.
content:
A forklift jib crane is an attachment that mounts on a forklift's carriage or forks and adds a boom and hook. With it, the truck can lift, reach and place loads the way a small crane does. It is one of the quickest ways to add crane capability to a warehouse, factory or yard without buying a separate crane. The attachment must be matched to the forklift and used within its load chart.

This guide explains the two main types of forklift jib crane, how to read capacity against reach, how to size one to your truck, and what the rules say about adding one. Specifications quoted below come from the BOB-LIFT forklift fly jib crane range.

Key Takeaways

  • A forklift jib crane adds a boom and hook to an existing forklift, giving it crane-style reach over obstacles, into pits and onto upper floors.
  • Hydraulic fly jib cranes fold and telescope using the forklift's hydraulic supply. Simple fork jibs are fixed or manually extended steel booms with no hydraulics.
  • Rated capacity applies only at short reach. On a moment-rated crane, available load falls in inverse proportion to the hook's distance from the mast: double the reach, roughly half the load.
  • Size the attachment to the forklift, not just the load: check the truck's rated capacity, mast height, hydraulic flow and the combined weight of the attachment.
  • In the United States, OSHA requires the forklift manufacturer's written approval and an updated capacity plate before a non-factory attachment is used.

What is a forklift jib crane?

A forklift jib crane is a lifting attachment that converts a counterbalance forklift into a mobile crane. The forklift supplies the travel, the mast lift and the counterweight. The jib supplies horizontal reach and a hook, so loads can be picked from above and lowered into places that forks cannot reach.

Buyers use the term for two quite different products, and the difference decides what you can actually lift.

Simple fork-mounted jibs

A simple fork jib is a steel boom that slides over the forks and is pinned or chained to the carriage. The boom is fixed or extended by hand in steps, and a hook or swivel hook hangs from the tip. It has no hydraulics of its own. Height comes only from raising the mast, and the angle of the boom does not change.

These attachments are low-cost and easy to fit. They suit occasional, light lifts at short reach, such as moving a die or lifting a coil from a rack.

Hydraulic forklift fly jib cranes

A forklift fly jib crane is a hydraulic crane mounted on the forklift's carriage. It has its own lift and fold cylinders and a telescopic boom, and it runs on hydraulic oil supplied by the forklift. The operator can raise the boom angle, fold it and extend it, so the hook can travel up, out and over obstacles independently of the mast.

BOB-LIFT's forklift fly jib cranes belong to this second group. The range runs from 2.3 t to 7 t maximum capacity, all rated at a 20 MPa working pressure, with maximum working distances from 5.4 m to 15.2 m.

Where does a forklift jib crane make sense?

A forklift jib crane makes sense wherever a forklift is already on site and the job needs lift from above, reach over an obstacle, or placement into a space the forks cannot enter. It is not a replacement for a mobile crane on heavy lifts, but it covers much of the routine lifting that would otherwise wait for a crane or be done unsafely with chains on forks.

Typical applications include:

  • Loading onto upper floors and mezzanines. The boom reaches over a guardrail or through an opening and sets a load down on the floor above. BOB-LIFT's product notes describe lifting irregular objects to higher floors as a core use.
  • Working in pits and below grade. A jib can lower a pump, motor or valve into a pit or trench where forks cannot follow.
  • Indoor lifting in confined spaces. A compact attachment can work inside factory halls and narrow aisles where a truck-mounted crane cannot fit or set its outriggers.
  • Handling irregular loads. Engines, castings, machine parts, bundled pipe and bagged material that do not sit on a pallet are easier to lift from a hook.
  • Logistics and construction yards. One forklift can switch between pallet work and crane work during a shift.

If the lifting point is on a public road or far from any forklift, a knuckle boom truck mounted crane is usually the better tool. For very tight indoor access, a spider crane is another option worth comparing.

How much can a forklift jib crane lift? Capacity versus reach

The headline capacity of a forklift jib crane applies only when the hook is close to the mast. As the boom reaches out, available capacity drops, and at full reach it is a fraction of the rated figure. Buyers who size by headline capacity often come up short at reach.

Why capacity falls with reach

Hydraulic fly jib cranes are rated by maximum lifting moment, measured in kN·m. Lifting moment is load multiplied by distance. A crane with a fixed moment rating can therefore carry a heavy load close in, or a light load far out, but not a heavy load far out.

A quick estimate is: load (t) ≈ lifting moment (kN·m) ÷ working distance (m) ÷ 9.81.

Take the 2.3 ton forklift fly jib crane. It has a 50 kN·m maximum lifting moment. Dividing 50 by its 2.3 t rating and by 9.81 gives about 2.2 m, so the headline capacity applies only up to roughly that distance. At its 5.4 m maximum working distance, the same moment gives about 0.9 t.

The table below applies that estimate to all four BOB-LIFT models, using the published specifications. It is an upper bound for planning only. The manufacturer's load chart for the specific configuration always governs, and the forklift's own stability can limit the lift before the crane does.

2.5 t fly jib crane (CC105) 2,500 kg 50 kN·m 6.6 m about 0.8 t 650 kg 3.5 or 4 t
3.5 t fly jib crane (CC125) 3,500 kg 60 kN·m 8.0 m about 0.8 t 850 kg 4 or 6 t

*Estimate = maximum lifting moment ÷ maximum working distance ÷ 9.81, rounded. It ignores boom self-weight and forklift stability, so real figures at full reach will be lower. The headline capacity applies only up to the distance where this estimate falls to the rated load; for the 2.5 t model that is about 2.0 m. Use the official load chart for any lift plan.

The pattern is clear. Moving up a model buys you much more reach and more capacity at mid-range, but the load at full extension stays around one tonne. If your job is "2 t at 6 m", you need the crane whose load chart shows 2 t at 6 m, which is not the same as a crane labeled 2 t.

Lifting height

Hook height depends on the forklift mast as well as the crane. BOB-LIFT lists maximum lifting height from the ground for two common mast (gantry) heights. With a 3 m mast, figures run from 8.4 m for the 2.3 t model to 11.0 m for the 3.5 t model. With a 4.5 m mast, they run from 9.9 m to 12.5 m. The 7 t model is listed at up to 19 m. Confirm the figure for your exact mast when you request a quote.

How to match a jib crane to your forklift

A forklift jib crane must be sized to the forklift as much as to the load. The attachment adds weight far forward of the front axle, and the truck must carry that weight, the load and the turning force of the boom without tipping.

Work through these checks before you order:

  1. Forklift rated capacity. Every BOB-LIFT fly jib is specified for a class of forklift. The 2.3 t model suits 3 to 3.5 t trucks, the 2.5 t model 3.5 to 4 t trucks, the 3.5 t model 4 to 6 t trucks, and the 7 t model needs a 10 t truck. Choosing a smaller truck than listed reduces stability and usable capacity.
  2. Attachment self-weight. The crane itself weighs 560 kg to 2,000 kg. That weight comes straight off the forklift's residual capacity before any load is lifted.
  3. Load center and residual capacity. The forklift manufacturer can calculate the truck's residual capacity with the attachment fitted. Ask for it in writing and compare it with the crane's load chart. The lower of the two is your real limit.
  4. Hydraulic supply. A hydraulic fly jib needs pressure and flow from the forklift's auxiliary circuit. BOB-LIFT models are rated at 20 MPa and 40 to 80 L/min depending on size. Check that your truck has a spare auxiliary valve section and enough pump flow, or plan for an added circuit.
  5. Mast height and overhead clearance. A taller mast gives more hook height but can conflict with doors, roof beams and racking. Measure the building, not just the job.
  6. Carriage class and mounting. Confirm the carriage width and class so the crane base locks securely to the truck.
  7. Floor and ground conditions. Heavy loads at reach concentrate force on the front wheels. Soft ground, slopes and pit edges need extra care or a lower rating.

Send these details with your inquiry and BOB-LIFT can recommend a model and configuration. You can start with a quote request or contact the engineering team.

Safety and compliance: what the rules say

Adding a jib crane to a forklift changes its capacity and how it behaves, so most safety regimes treat it as a modification that needs approval and new capacity markings.

In the United States, OSHA's powered industrial truck standard is 29 CFR 1910.178. Paragraph (a)(4) states that modifications and additions which affect capacity and safe operation must not be made by the user without the manufacturer's prior written approval. Capacity, operation and maintenance plates must then be changed accordingly (29 CFR 1910.178, Legal Information Institute). Paragraph (a)(5) adds that a truck fitted with non-factory front-end attachments must be marked to identify the attachment and show the approximate weight of the truck and attachment combination.

OSHA has confirmed in a standard interpretation that a front-end attachment is generally an "addition" under this rule, so both the written approval and the new marking are required before use (OSHA standard interpretation, 2002). Other countries apply similar principles through their own machinery and lifting regulations. Check local requirements before the attachment goes into service.

Practical rules that apply everywhere:

  • Use the load chart, every lift. Know the weight of the load and the working distance, then read the chart.
  • Travel with the load low and the boom retracted. A swinging load shifts the combined center of gravity and can tip the truck, especially on turns or slopes.
  • Keep people clear. Never let anyone stand or walk under a raised boom or a suspended load.
  • Inspect before each shift. Check pins, hoses, cylinders, hook latch and mounting locks.
  • Train operators for crane work. Driving a forklift and rigging a suspended load are different skills.

Why choose a BOB-LIFT forklift fly jib crane?

BOB-LIFT builds hydraulic cranes for trucks, ships and forklifts, and the forklift fly jib range applies the same folding and telescopic boom design to a carriage-mounted package. Buyers get:

  • Four sizes from 2.3 t to 7 t, with published lifting moment, reach, height, self-weight and matched forklift class for each model.
  • Folding, telescopic booms that reach over obstacles, into pits and onto upper floors, which a fixed fork jib cannot do.
  • Compact packages for indoor work, designed for confined spaces and narrow areas.
  • Factory-direct supply and export support, with technical data, photos and pre-order communication for international buyers. See how the equipment is built on the BOB-LIFT factory tour.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a forklift jib and a forklift fly jib crane?

A forklift jib is usually a fixed or manually extended steel boom that slips over the forks and has no hydraulics. A forklift fly jib crane is a hydraulic crane with its own cylinders and a folding, telescopic boom, powered by the forklift's hydraulic circuit. The fly jib can change boom angle and reach while loaded, so it can lift over obstacles and into pits.

Can any forklift use a jib crane attachment?

No. The forklift must have enough rated capacity, a suitable carriage and, for hydraulic models, an auxiliary hydraulic supply. Each BOB-LIFT model lists its matched forklift class, from 3 t trucks for the smallest model to a 10 t truck for the 7 t model. The forklift manufacturer should confirm residual capacity with the attachment fitted.

How far can a forklift jib crane reach?

BOB-LIFT fly jib cranes have maximum working distances from 5.4 m on the 2.3 ton model to 15.2 m on the 7 ton model. Capacity at full reach is much lower than the rated maximum, so always check the load chart for the distance you need.

Do I need approval to fit a jib crane to my forklift?

In the United States, yes. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(a)(4) requires the forklift manufacturer's prior written approval for additions that affect capacity or safe operation, and the capacity plate must be updated. Other regions have comparable rules, so check with your local authority.

Is a forklift jib crane cheaper than a truck-mounted crane?

It is usually a lower investment because it uses a forklift you already own for travel, lift and counterweight. The total cost depends on the model size, whether the forklift needs an added auxiliary hydraulic circuit or a larger truck, mounting work, and freight. It suits on-site and indoor lifting. For a price on your configuration, request a quote with your forklift model and lifting requirement. For road travel between sites or heavier lifts at long reach, a truck mounted crane remains the better choice.

Choosing the right forklift jib crane

A forklift jib crane gives an existing forklift real crane capability: reach, hook height and the ability to place loads where forks cannot go. The key decisions are the type of jib, the load you need at the reach you need, and whether your forklift can carry the attachment safely.

  • Choose a hydraulic fly jib when you need to lift over obstacles, into pits or onto upper floors.
  • Size by the load chart at your working distance, not by the headline capacity.
  • Match the crane to the forklift's capacity, carriage and hydraulic supply, and get the approvals and new capacity plate in place.
